english: 2.) Proof of Fermat's theorem for the case that the class number of the field k(l-th root of 1) is divisible by l but not by l^2 (perhaps also by l^2), by my simpler method, assuming the reciprocity laws for l-th power residues.
topic: A list of research and dissertation topics: the discriminant and invariants of the quartic, Poincaré cycles of differential equations, rotation of a body filled with fluid, three number-theoretic doctoral topics (class fields, Fermat's theorem, Weber's theorem), and independence of the laws 1-17 for complex number systems.

triage.modern_statement: Let l be an odd prime and h the class number of the cyclotomic field Q(ζ_l). Suppose l divides h but l^2 does not (an irregular prime, at least in a weak sense; Hilbert also wonders whether l^2 | h could be allowed). The task is to prove Fermat's Last Theorem x^l + y^l = z^l for such l, assuming the l-th power reciprocity laws (essentially class field theory for Q(ζ_l)). The proof should extend Hilbert's own simplified version of Kummer's proof for regular primes, which is in his Zahlbericht. This is a proposed doctoral topic: carry Kummer-style arguments from regular primes to irregular primes where the l-part of the class group is small.
triage.answered_by: I could not identify a dissertation that carried out this exact topic. The underlying mathematics was dealt with by others. Kummer (1857) had already given sufficient criteria for some irregular primes, including 37, 59 and 67. Furtwängler (1912) used class field theory and Eisenstein's reciprocity law to prove criteria for the first case of FLT; this is the 'assume the reciprocity laws' approach that Hilbert describes. Vandiver (Trans. AMS, 1929) and his later computer work (1954, all primes up to 2521) extended Kummer's method to irregular primes. The whole question was made moot when Wiles and Taylor–Wiles proved Fermat's Last Theorem for all exponents (Annals of Mathematics, May 1995).

evidence.claim: Kummer proved FLT for regular primes. In 1857 he improved the result by giving irregular-pair criteria for the first case. The irregular primes below 100 are 37, 59 and 67, with h_37 = 37, so 37 divides h but 37^2 does not.
h_37 = 37, h_59 = 3·59·233 and h_67 = 67·12739. These are all cases where l divides h but l^2 does not, which is exactly the situation in Hilbert's note.
In 1912 Furtwängler used class field theory (reciprocity laws) to derive criteria for the first case of FLT. As corollaries he gave new proofs of Wieferich's and Mirimanoff's theorems.
Furtwängler's paper is 'Letzter Fermatscher Satz und Eisenstein'sches Reziprozitätsgesetz', Sitzungsber. Akad. Wiss. Wien 121 (1912).
Vandiver, 'On Fermat's Last Theorem', Trans. AMS 31 (1929), gives criteria for FLT at irregular primes.
Kummer's approach was later extended to irregular primes by computation. In 1954 Vandiver proved FLT for all primes up to 2521.
Wiles's 1995 papers in the Annals of Mathematics completed the proof of Fermat's Last Theorem.

triage.why: The note is clearly a research or dissertation topic: Kummer's FLT proof extended to irregular primes whose class number is divisible by l but not by l^2, using reciprocity laws. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems. Others did research in this direction: Kummer had already done some of it in 1857, Furtwängler used reciprocity laws in 1912, and Vandiver followed. Wiles's 1995 proof then settled FLT in full, so this special-case program is obsolete. Confidence is medium for two reasons. First, I found no source showing whether a Hilbert student wrote this dissertation or what his 'simpler method' produced in this case. Second, the sources do not show whether Hilbert's exact formulation (with or without the l^2 extension) was ever proved as stated by that method.
